A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research, with SL-SLR renamed SSL-SLR. All 15 pages of v1 and 21 pages of v2 were inspected, including figures, equations, tables, and references. Neither contains a separate appendix, and no material reading gaps prevent comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original recognition, cross-language transfer, semi-supervised, embedding, and ablation results across five sign-language datasets.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds boundary-selection failure analyses and execution-time comparisons.

M1.justification: The three-branch SL-FPN architecture, original-sample input, three-term MSE objective, predictor, stop-gradient, and boundary-search pseudocode remain unchanged. Both versions describe permuting the first third and last quarter of sequences. Renaming the framework and explaining sampled boundary searches do not establish a changed method.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate LSFB, LSA, GSL, ASL Citizen, and WLASL-100/300, retaining isolated recognition, cross-language transfer, and limited-label evaluation. The new analyses use existing datasets. Continuous recognition and broader computer-vision applications are discussed but not experimentally evaluated.

E2.justification: v2 Table 6 adds SignRep (avg) and SignRep (weighted) to the ASL Citizen comparison previously containing SignCLIP and the proposed method. Other recognition comparators remain. The new timing comparison uses the already-evaluated SimSiam and BYOL methods.

E3.justification: The reported contrastive temperature changes from 0.1 to 0.5. v2 introduces dataset-dependent scratch/pretraining descriptions where v1 specified initialization from Fink's weights and pretraining. PCA attribution becomes a UMAP-cited visualization description, despite identical embedding images. The ablation accuracy horizon extends from 900 to 1400 epochs, and new analyses compare global versus sign-specific boundaries and execution time. These are reported protocol revisions, without establishing that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 Figures 4–5 add substantial analyses of boundary heterogeneity and accuracy losses from applying global boundaries to failure cases. The direct interior-versus-edge permutation control in v1 Figure 4 is removed. v2 also adds timing comparisons, reports that loss-term weighting had little effect, and revises the collapse/original-input ablation plots.

E5.justification: Section 5.2 newly states that SL-FPN was trained five consecutive times for each tested permutation. This discloses a run count without establishing an increase in runs. The main evaluation's eight runs and 95% confidence reporting remain unchanged.

E6.justification: v2 adds boundary-distribution, failure-loss, timing, and SignRep results, replaces ablation trajectories, and removes the interior-permutation results. Proposed-method ASL Citizen top-1 changes from 48.56% in v1 Table 5 to 47.06% in v2 Table 6; top-5 remains 78.96%. Added weighted SignRep leads with 49.95%/80.09%. Tables 1–3 and inertia values remain identical. The revised scores do not establish a same-setting performance change.

T1.justification: Section 5.2 adds an elementary boundary-search cost calculation, 2kT, based on the number of tests, execution time per test, and two search directions. The loss definitions and mathematical structure of Algorithm 1 remain unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The two-component contribution and claims of improved recognition, transfer, and limited-label learning remain. v2 removes the introduction's explicit claim of attaining state-of-the-art results without large amounts of data from diverse sources, modestly narrowing the advertised advantage.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly discusses signs whose informative frames violate the global boundary choice, resulting losses, sensitivity, and computational costs. It replaces the uniformly favorable embedding interpretation with an acknowledgment that LSFB instances remain scattered. It also adds runtime explanations and proposed applicability to semantic inconsistency and continuous recognition, without corresponding new task evaluations.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the sampled boundary-search grid, distinguishes the 700-class LSFB state-of-the-art comparison from 500-class linear evaluation, and identifies Lucia computational resources. PyTorch changes from version 2.6 to 2.4, and the explicit pretrained-weight initialization statement disappears. These revise reproducibility information without establishing new dataset coverage.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of SignRep, YouTube-SL, and recent work by Gueuwou and colleagues, plus supporting references for semantic consistency, visualization, and training. Ferreira et al. is removed. These update and broaden the literature context while retaining the central positioning around negative-free learning and sign-specific augmentation.

P1.justification: The framework is renamed SSL-SLR, author ordering changes, and prose receives copyediting and localized explanatory reorganization, particularly in Sections 5 and 6. An acknowledgments section is added. The main section sequence and narrative structure remain recognizable.

P2.justification: A new document template changes the title/author block, typography, spacing, and float placement throughout. Figure 1 blurs faces; the interior-permutation figure is replaced by two diagnostic figures; a timing table is added; and ablation curves, axes, and legends are redrawn. Retained tables and embedding panels are relocated or renumbered.

improvement.justification: v2 improves transparency through failure-case analyses, stronger SignRep comparisons, and a more qualified interpretation of the unchanged LSFB embeddings. Timing evidence also helps assess computational tradeoffs. These gains are limited by removal of the interior-permutation control and unresolved reporting inconsistencies: Sections 6 and 6.4 differ on pretraining, while the timing prose describes self-supervised training but Table 4 labels linear evaluation. Overall, the evidence supports a modest improvement.
